title: Robust Reputation-Driven Crowdsourced Federated Learning

C-a.quote: At each FL round t, the aggregator collects a set of local updates Θt = {θ1t , . . . , θnt }. Each update is first embedded into a vector space and processed through a two-stage robust pipeline: ... (2) Robust Multi-Krum Selection. After mixing, a robust selection is applied: t Ctrusted = MultiKrum({θ̃it }), (5) which selects the subset of updates minimizing pairwise distances. This step provides guarantees against Byzantine behaviors under bounded adversarial assumptions [1].
C-a.locator: Section 3.4 R2-NNM Filtering; the two stages are applied to the same round in sequence and each carries its own defense purpose. Stage 1, reputation-aware nearest-neighbor mixing: "This step acts as a geometric denoising operator designed to reduce the influence of isolated or adversarial updates while preserving local consensus structures.". Stage 2, the fixed downstream rule: "(2) Robust Multi-Krum Selection. After mixing, a robust selection is applied: t Ctrusted = MultiKrum({θ̃it }), (5) which selects the subset of updates minimizing pairwise distances. This step provides guarantees against Byzantine behaviors under bounded adversarial assumptions [1].". The reputation model is a third defense-purposed component acting within the same round, because the mixing weights are functions of the current local reputation scores, and its purpose is stated in the Abstract, "The proposed mechanism prevents stealthy attackers from gradually accumulating trust and influencing future tasks.", and in Section 1, "R2CFL introduces a novel reputation model that is tightly coupled with a detect-and-filter aggregation strategy, namely robust nearest neighbor mixing (R2-NNM).". No Amendment 3 excision is needed. A crowdsourcing co-purpose for the reputation model (worker selection, incentives, rewards) is present and is recorded rather than relied on, since the defense purpose is stated independently

C-b.quote: Unlike classical defenses (e.g., FLAME or DeepSight), R2-NNM introduces a closed-loop interaction between reputation and robustness: reputation influences filtering, and filtering in turn shapes reputation. Consequently, participants that are consistently rejected by the robust filtering stage experience a progressive loss of influence, while consistently accepted participants accumulate trust. This feedback mechanism makes it significantly more difficult for adversaries to progressively infiltrate the system through repeated unsuccessful attempts.
C-b.locator: Section 3.4; the pairing reason is BIDIRECTIONAL and both directions are stated in the quoted sentence. Reputation supplies the memoryless geometric filter with temporal memory, so that repeated rejection costs an adversary influence; the filter supplies the reputation model with a signal that cannot be manipulated the way performance-based signals can, which is the deficiency the paper names for single-mechanism alternatives, "While convenient, these mechanisms become unreliable in stealthy adversarial settings, where the underlying signals can be manipulated through sophisticated attacks such as backdoor attacks [30, 31] and strategic model poisoning [25].". The consequence is stated as a property of the pair rather than of either constituent, "reputation becomes an empirical estimate of the probability of being consistently selected by a robust aggregation rule."

Bold = best on both or FPR, brown = 2nd best (TPR higher is better, FPR lower is better; DeepSight excluded from ranking as it detects nothing)."

C-d.quote: Figure 3 (top sub-figures) sweeps k ... for R2-NNM and NNM. As k increases both methods exhibit a clear improvement in fairness, with FPR decreasing significantly (0.28 → 0.12). This regime reflects the benefit of stronger mixing, which reduces update variance, improves convergence stability, and enhances separation between benign and malicious contributions. Slight variations in TPR (∆TPR ≤ 0.02) are observed within the acceptable mixing range (k ≤ 10), indicating that moderate mixing has only a limited impact on detection performance. Beyond this range, however, TPR degrades (down to 0.94) despite a further reduction in FPR (< 0.12). This behavior suggests an over-smoothing effect, where excessive mixing increases conservativeness at the expense of detection sensitivity.

coder_note:
THE CLOSEST EXTERNAL ANALOGUE TO OUR OWN SCREEN IN THE ENTIRE FRAME, AND A3 MUST NAME IT BEFORE A REVIEWER FINDS IT. Figure 3's top panel is a two-family, five-rung ladder: two upstream mixing designs (reputation-aware R2-NNM and uniform NNM) crossed with a graded dose (k = 3, 5, 8, 10, 12 in the legend), one fixed downstream mechanism (Multi-Krum), one fixed attack, and the downstream stage's own decisions read at every rung. That is structurally the design of our controlled family. It is closer than EnCAgg (2605.22506), which varies presence versus absence rather than a graded family, and closer than Secure-CHG (2606.31066), which measures the downstream signal under exactly two upstream conditions. WHAT OUR CONTRIBUTION ADDS, stated so A3 can state it rather than leave the omission to be read as agreement with the novelty charge: (i) their graded family is a parameter of their OWN upstream stage, so nothing in the sweep can reorder two different defenses -- the two curves are their own method and its ablated form, not two defenses being compared; (ii) they read a single design's operating point, never an ORDERING across defense arms, which is the quantity our Proposition is about; (iii) the sweep chooses an operating range -- the paper's conclusion is that mixing up to k = 10 is acceptable -- rather than drawing an identification conclusion from the dependence; (iv) one attack, one dataset, no intervals over seeds. The dependence they find is real and NON-MONOTONE, which supports rather than undercuts our attenuation story, and A4 should cite it as external evidence that an upstream stage's setting moves a fixed downstream rule's decisions.

c_d_route AMENDED IN-SESSION FROM component-contrast TO hyperparameter-sweep under the tie-break rule adopted on DP-BR-FedAvg (2609.03064): when a row satisfies more than one C-d route, the field records the graded-dose route if one exists and the locator records the other. This row has both -- five settings of the upstream mixing parameter AND a substitution between two upstream families -- and the rule resolves it mechanically rather than by judging which finding the paper calls central. Both routes remain stated in the C-d locator and neither the code nor anything downstream of it changes.

TABLE 2 IS A SIMULATED COMPOSITION, NOT A MEASURED ONE, AND IT IS THE SHARPEST EXHIBIT THE AUDIT HAS FOUND FOR OUR THESIS. The Abstract's second claim is a composition claim across upstream defenses -- "Furthermore, when integrated with existing detect-and-filter defenses, the proposed reputation model faithfully captures the statistical robustness of the underlying defense by producing reputation scores that closely reflect its true positive and false positive characteristics." -- and Table 2 appears to deliver it, reporting the downstream reputation model's separation gap for M-Krum, NNM, FLAME, DeepSight, AutoDFL, SSMTD and R2-NNM under a fixed attack, "Table 2: Final Ltrep,i scores at round 100 under A3FL (the worst-case scenario).". But Section 4.3 says how it was obtained: "For each trainer i, we simulate the robust local evaluation (Eq. (10)) over multiple FL rounds. The stochastic reliability indicator Reliableti is sampled using the defense-specific TPR and FPR: P[Reliableti = 1 | i ∈ B] = 1− FPR, P[Reliableti = 1 | i ∈ M] = 1− TPR. (14) This models the probability that a benign or malicious trainer is considered trustworthy by the defense.". The upstream defense is replaced by its measured (TPR, FPR) pair and the downstream reputation dynamics are driven by independent Bernoulli draws from those two scalars. So the composition is ASSUMED to factor through the upstream stage's two marginal rates, independently across clients and rounds, which is the strongest possible form of the composition invariance our Proposition denies -- adopted as a modelling convenience and never tested. The paper then reads the result as confirmation: "Overall, these trends align with TPR/FPR behavior: strong defenses ensure fast malicious decay and stable benign retention, whereas weaker ones reduce or lose discrimination, confirming the consistency of the reputation dynamics with theoretical expectations.". A4 can use this in one sentence: the frame contains a paper that varies the upstream stage across seven defenses, holds the downstream fixed, and never runs the composition, because it assumes the interaction away. I coded C-d on the k sweep, which is a real run, and NOT on Table 2; rule 4 would arguably admit Table 2 as a modelled route, but the honest stratification puts it with the analytic treatments and this note is the disclosure. It is also the frame's TENTH external treatment of composition invariance and the first MODELLED one -- neither analytic (it proves nothing) nor empirical (it measures nothing about the composition).

A FOURTH STRUCTURAL KIND FOR A5'S PARALLEL-VERSUS-SEQUENTIAL AXIS, AND IT IS A REAL LIMIT ON OUR OWN FRAMING. The composition here is a CLOSED LOOP: "Unlike classical defenses (e.g., FLAME or DeepSight), R2-NNM introduces a closed-loop interaction between reputation and robustness: reputation influences filtering, and filtering in turn shapes reputation. Consequently, participants that are consistently rejected by the robust filtering stage experience a progressive loss of influence, while consistently accepted participants accumulate trust. This feedback mechanism makes it significantly more difficult for adversaries to progressively infiltrate the system through repeated unsuccessful attempts.". Reputation modulates the mixing weights within round t, and the filter's acceptance decisions update reputation at the end of round t, so the same component is downstream within a round and upstream in the next. Our identification argument presupposes that upstream and downstream are fixed roles; under feedback they are not, and holding the downstream fixed while varying the upstream is not even well posed across rounds. A5 should record this as a scope condition on Prop. prop:identification_full rather than as a property of this paper. The axis now has four kinds: parallel, fixed-sequential, conditionally routed (Secure-CHG) and closed-loop (R2CFL).

C-b IS BIDIRECTIONAL, WHICH IS A NEW SHAPE RATHER THAN A NEW KIND. Residual coverage (RKD) has one direction: the upstream leaves a residue and the downstream exists to catch it. Here each constituent supplies what the other lacks -- temporal memory in one direction, a manipulation-resistant signal in the other -- so the pairing reason is symmetric. FedSurrogate's Stage 2 was bidirectional in what it CORRECTED (residual adversaries and misclassified benign clients); this is bidirectional in WHICH CONSTITUENT BENEFITS. A5 should report it as a symmetric form of complementary coverage and note that it is the only such instance in the frame.

DOMAIN NOTE: the frame's first crowdsourced-FL and first blockchain/oracle deployment paper. Its inclusion is correct under the frozen screen -- it proposes and evaluates a defense pipeline against poisoning -- and it is useful because the reputation stage would look like an incentive mechanism from its name alone, which is the configuration Amendment 3 exists for; here, as on Fedward, LASA and RKD, the amendment RAISES rather than lowers the code.

TWO SMALLER OBSERVATIONS FOR A5. First, the paper excludes a baseline from a ranking and states the reason in the caption itself, "Table 1: Detection (TPR/FPR) performance under attacks. Bold = best on both or FPR, brown = 2nd best (TPR higher is better, FPR lower is better; DeepSight excluded from ranking as it detects nothing).", which is a piece of reporting hygiene worth noting beside the misaligned-attribution exhibits. Second, this is the frame's clearest SAME-PAPER pair on the same-stage question: the k sweep varies the upstream stage and reads the fixed downstream's decisions (admitted), while the alpha sweep varies the reputation stage and reads only that stage's own separation gap, "Table 6 sweeps α (Eq. (9)) over [0, 1] and reports the final separation gap ∆ between benign and malicious clients under IID and non-IID partitions." (declined). SecureAFL versus FedSurrogate made that contrast across two papers; here it is inside one, with everything else held constant, which is the better teaching example.
